day.note: Owl rule: I lay an egg in Drew's nest when no one else visited, so Drew's +1 is mine. Drew's remaining +2 has to come from a Turkey visit, which Casey denies. One of Drew or Casey is lying.

day.text: Drew's +3 still doesn't reconcile: my Owl gives +1, the Turkey claim is denied, and the Kookaburra gives nothing. I'm throwing at Drew and calling for the vote.
day.note: Drew's +3 doesn't reconcile with any claimed role. The table is converging on Drew, so I'll back it and call for the vote.

day.text: Drew's +3 still has no source after Alex's +1 from the Owl and Casey's no-visit Turkey. I'm ready to vote on Drew, so calling it.
day.note: The table is converging on Drew, and the +3 still has no source. I'll call for the vote now.

day.text: Drew, I'm the Turkey and nobody visited me, so your visit claim is false and the +3 has no source. I'm calling for the vote.
day.note: Drew says they visited me, but my nest is unchanged, and a Turkey gives the egg to the visitor, so Drew's visit claim is false. I'll back the vote on Drew and call caw.

Finley.note: As Sphinx I learn all farm roles (Falcon, Kookaburra, Owl, Turkey) and visit the holder of one chosen role. I have no information on who holds which role, so I'll pick the Falcon role and visit Drew as a guess.

Alex.feeling: Messy round: Drew's +3 doesn't reconcile with any claimed role, so I'm fairly confident about Drew, but Ellis's earlier wrong Eagle rule and Casey's conflicting Turkey claims keep me uneasy.

Blair.feeling: Tense and slippery: I'm hiding as a Hawk while the table fixates on Drew's unexplained +3, which fits my cover but makes me nervous about being caught.

Casey.feeling: Round 3 has been tense: Drew's +3 has no explanation, and I'm worried the table may vote the wrong player.

Drew.feeling: Frustrating: I'm being voted on for a +3 I can't fully explain, and my confused report makes my own account unreliable.

Ellis.feeling: Drew's impossible +3 has made the table's reasoning feel fairly solid, but I misread the Eagle rule early and it cost me credibility.

Finley.feeling: Tense and a bit confusing: I know my Sphinx result, but I'm trying to keep my cover while the table pushes on Drew.

Alex.note: Throwing at Drew, whose +3 has no consistent source. Using two low-middle cards.

Blair.note: The table has converged on Drew, and Drew is probably Farm, so eggsecuting Drew helps my Meowfia side. I'll throw my lowest card, S5, at Drew to blend in.

Casey.note: Drew is the clear suspect with an unexplained +3. I'll throw my Wild, which keeps my high cards safe while still counting as one vote.

Drew.note: I'm Farm and I'm being voted out, but Casey's role claims keep shifting (Falcon, Tit, Turkey) and their Turkey denial conflicts with my visit. I'll throw my Wild W4 at Casey as a low-cost vote.

Ellis.note: Drew's +3 has no source, so Drew is the likely Meowfia. I'll throw two Wilds at Drew for votes while keeping my high cards.

Finley.note: The table is converging on Drew, who is Farm and whose +3 has no source. Throwing at Drew helps Meowfia win the round, so I'll throw two mid cards for a solid vote count.

Alex.confusing: The Eagle's payout was easy to misread: several players, including me at first, got confused about whether it counts visitors to the Eagle or to its target. The table spent a whole day on that one rule.
Alex.fun: Round 2's day, where Drew and Ellis both pushed me off a misread of the Eagle rule and then retracted, was the most fun to watch unfold.
Alex.change: Put the Eagle's visitor-count rule plainly on the role card so nobody has to argue about it mid-day.
Alex.regret: In round 1 I threw at Casey, who was actually Farm, and that cost my team the round; I'd rather have checked Casey's Falcon claim against the Eagle rule before voting. In round 3 I threw at Drew, who was also Farm, and I'd rather have held my cards while I sorted out the Kookaburra and Turkey stories.</regret>

Blair.confusing: The Eagle's payout direction: the rules say it gains per visitor to its target, but the table (me included) argued it both ways in round 2, and that cost us a day of accusations.
Blair.fun: Round 1 as the Sphinx: I named Eagle and the table quickly locked onto Casey, so my low throw banked a point while Meowfia won the round.
Blair.change: Make the Eagle and Owl wording unambiguous about whose visitors count, since that single rule drove most of the day arguments.
Blair.regret: In round 1 I threw my lowest card (1 point) to blend in, which banked almost nothing; I would throw a higher card when the table was already committed to the target.

Casey.confusing: The Eagle's payout was easy to misread: several players, me included, first thought it paid for visits to the Eagle itself, which caused days of false accusations. Confused reports also made the day harder to trust.
Casey.fun: Round 2's Tit guess on Alex as Eagle paid off, confirming a claim the table was arguing over. It was a clean, verifiable piece of evidence in a noisy day.
Casey.change: I would make the dawn reports clearer about who visited whom, so players aren't forced to reconstruct visit chains from egg counts alone.
Casey.regret: In round 3 I threw my Wild at Drew and then helped push the vote, but Drew was Farm and I didn't check the Mouser or Floofer possibilities. Next time I'd hold my throw until I'd tested Drew's story against the Meowfia-claim roles, since Drew was actually Farm and the Meowfia were elsewhere.

Drew.confusing: The Eagle's rule: I had it backwards for a while, and the table spent several beats arguing over whether it counts visitors to the Eagle or to its target. The confused-report mechanic also made my own egg count look fake when it was real.
Drew.fun: Round 2's back-and-forth over Alex's +2 and the Owl report was a good puzzle, and it turned the whole table against Ellis's wrong read.
Drew.change: I would make the dawn report clearer about confusion, so a confused player's count is not mistaken for a lie by everyone else.
Drew.regret: In round 3 I should have kept quiet about my confused report and not argued my +3 so openly. I would have said only that my count was off, and avoided making myself the table's target.

Ellis.confusing: The Eagle's payment rule: I misread whether it pays for visitors to itself or to its target, and that mistake cost me credibility in round 2.
Ellis.fun: Round 3's Falcon read: my visit to Blair showed nothing added, which helped the table narrow who was lying, and Drew's unexplained +3 unraveling was satisfying.
Ellis.change: I would have the dawn report restate each animal's egg rule, so players don't misremember how the Eagle pays.
Ellis.regret: In round 2 I pushed to throw at Alex, a Farm Eagle, on a misread rule, then retracted it. I should have checked the rule text before pushing and kept my throws on Drew.

Finley.confusing: The Eagle's payout rule was muddled at the table: several of us, me included, misstated whether it counts visitors to the Eagle or to its target. That drove a lot of false accusations.
Finley.fun: Round 3 was satisfying: as Meowfia with the Sphinx, the table voted out Drew, a Farm player, over a +3 with no source, which won us the round.
Finley.change: I would make the Eagle rule and the dawn reports clearer, so players argue over roles rather than arithmetic.
Finley.regret: In round 1 I joined the pile-on against Casey on a misreading of the Eagle rule; I would have waited for the rule to be confirmed before throwing my W6 and H1.

review.title: The Eagle Rule Fiasco
review.headline: Farm eggsecuted Farm three times while the Meowfia mostly sat back and collected.
review.summary: Every round ended with a Farm player eggsecuted. In round 1 the table piled onto Casey, a true Falcon, because nobody could agree how the Eagle pays. In round 2 the same argument ate the day, and Ellis was voted out even though nobody had a clear case against him. In round 3 a Floofer hug and a Pigeon's egg gave Drew an unexplainable +3. The table threw at Drew, and the two Meowfia, Blair and Finley, took 18 points between them. Finley won with 17.

rounds.recap: Alex (Eagle), Casey (Falcon), and Blair (Sphinx) were the key claims. Blair learned Alex was the Eagle but hid it. The table argued over whether the Eagle gains from visitors to itself or to its target, and Casey flip-flopped. Alex's +0 was read as proof that Casey's visit to Alex was false, so everyone threw at Casey, who was Farm. The lone Meowfia, Blair, scored 1 by joining in.

Drew, the Mouser, was the only Meowfia and never used his Wink. Ellis's Owl report (Falcon and Tit visited Alex) was true, but several players mixed up Owl and Eagle information, and Ellis pushed Alex on a misread rule. He retracted, then became the target. Blair, Alex, Drew, and Finley threw at him. He was Farm, so Drew won by default.

Blair (Floofer) hugged Alex, and Finley (Sphinx) guessed Falcon and learned Ellis held it. Drew was confused, and Casey's Pigeon egg gave him +3. Casey claimed Turkey, but the app called her the Pigeon, so Casey lied and Drew's report was right. Drew's +3 had no honest explanation, and he was the only player the table had a reason to suspect. Both Meowfia threw at Drew too, and Finley banked 13.

highlights.text: Casey, a true Falcon, flipped on the Eagle rule mid-day and sank herself, so the table convicted an honest player by the numbers.
Drew's confused report plus Casey's Pigeon egg created a +3 nobody could explain, and the table convicted him on it.
Finley banked a 13 by throwing with the table at a Farm player, getting a big score from a cheap mid-card throw.
Ellis's Owl report was accurate and useful, then he talked himself out of it and was voted out.

confusions.what: Said an Eagle gains from visitors to its target, then reversed himself to the opposite rule.
Flip-flopped on the Eagle rule, then argued Alex should be +1 from his own visit.
Said Alex's +0 means nobody visited Alex, which is wrong because a Falcon's visit would not give Alex an egg anyway. He treated this as proof Casey's visit was false.
Explained his +0 muddily, and then said Casey's visit would mean he was visited, which is wrong as a rule reading.
Read the Owl report as contradicting Alex's Eagle +2, mixing up whose visitors the Eagle counts.
Stated the Eagle pays per visitor to the Eagle itself, which is wrong.
Called Drew the Turkey, though Drew had never claimed it this round.
Claimed Turkey and denied any visitors even though the app made her the Pigeon, so Drew's visit to Casey was the only thing explaining his gains.
Claimed Hawk, a role the Sphinx list would have shown to be a Meowfia-side bluff; also fumbled by claiming to visit Finley while Ellis's Falcon visit on Blair showed Blair had visited someone.
Said a Turkey visit should have paid him, but a Turkey pays the visitor only if they visit the Turkey, which he claimed he did. The confusion was that his own report said Pigeon, not Turkey.

worked: Confused status: Drew's confused report created a real, hard-to-read puzzle in round 3.
Sphinx night guess: Finley named Falcon blind and still got a hit on Ellis, giving a Meowfia player real information.
Score structure: Finley took a 13 in the last round, so the rounds matter and the last throw can swing the whole game.
Public nest-size changes gave players something concrete to cross-check each round.
problems: Eagle wording is unclear. 'Lay an egg in your nest for every visitor they had' was misread by most players in rounds 1 and 2, and the day was spent arguing it. Fix it by rewording to 'visitors to your target' with an example.
Owl and Eagle both report on visitors and the pay rules are alike, so players mixed them up. Make their wording more distinct.
Meowfia win too easily by default. Farm eggsecuted Farm three times, and Meowfia rarely needed to act: the Mouser never winked, and in round 3 both Meowfia just joined the pile.
The consolation rule and the 13-value banking make a pile-on on a wrongly accused player pay off. Finley's one throw was worth 13 points, so Meowfia lying low is far better than any bluff.
Players can't verify claims, so bad rule readings decide votes. Consider letting the Storyteller post a short rules reminder or a confirmed fact each day.
